text: Education begins with stories, since children hear stories before they ever train their bodies. For that reason the founders of the city must supervise the makers of stories, and Socrates gives Glaucon two laws for speech about the gods in Republic II. The first is that God is good, and, being good, is the cause only of good things. Since the evils in the world far outnumber the goods, some other cause must be found for them, because nothing good can cause harm. This rule excludes Homer's story of the two jars at Zeus's threshold, along with every poet who makes a god responsible for the ruin of a household. The second law is that God neither changes nor deceives. Whatever is in the best condition is least altered by outside forces, and a perfect being would never willingly exchange its condition for the worse. Stories of gods who change their shape therefore have no place in the city's education. The lie hated most by gods and human beings is not the spoken lie but the lie in the soul: to be deceived about reality in the most important part of oneself. A god has no such lie within, and no motive to put one in anyone else's soul.
